 Toyota issues voluntary Takata airbag recall on 314,000 vehicles
 By Lurah Lowery 
 on November 18, 2026 
 Announcements 
 Share This: Toyota is conducting a voluntary safety recall involving 314,000 Toyota and Lexus vehicles in the U.S. equipped with Takata front passenger airbags.
 Takata, a bankrupt parts supplier , was responsible for manufacturing airbag canisters in defective airbag inflators that can explode and spray sharp metal fragments toward the driver and passengers, comparable to shrapnel from an exploding grenade, which has caused severe injuries and deaths.
 The Takata airbag inflator recall is the largest safety recall in automotive history and spans worldwide. Issues first came to light in 2008. Vehicles across more than 30 brands are equipped with the airbags , according to NHTSA.
 NHTSA says the airbags have killed 28 people and caused at least 400 injuries in the U.S. It linked the 28th death to an incident that occurred in Alabama involving a Honda vehicle.
 Toyota says it will replace the front passenger airbag inflator or airbag assembly, depending on the model, for all involved vehicles, free of charge.
 A Nov. 12 Toyota press release about the recall doesn’t list the specific vehicle models involved. Instead, it directs owners to visit Toyota.com/recall or NHTSA.gov/recalls and enter their VIN or license plate information to check for recalls.
 Toyota’s Takata recall page lists several vehicle models; however, it isn’t clear which, if any, are involved in the newest recall. The page states, “If you own a Toyota, Scion, or Lexus manufactured between 2002 and 2017, your vehicle may be subject to a Safety Recall for the Takata Front Passenger Airbag Inflator or Takata Driver’s Airbag Inflator.”
 Toyota doesn’t provide a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) campaign number for the newest recall, which is necessary to look up the full affected vehicle population on NHTSA’s site. NHTSA’s Takata recall page doesn’t show when it was last updated, so it’s unclear if the vehicle lists include the new recall population.
 In October, NHTSA said it “cannot confirm the status” of the remaining 9% of more than 67 million recalled Takata airbags , or whether they remain on U.S. roads.
 NHTSA categorizes each U.S. state and territory into one of three recall zones based on temperature and humidity. Toyota’s Takata page states that vehicles in Zone A, areas with high temperature cycling and humidity, could experience significant propellant degradation after six to nine years of service. Some models listed on the page date back to model year 2002.
 Toyota’s Takata page lists Zone B vehicles, areas with moderate temperature cycling and humidity, as being in service for an estimated 10-15 years before degradation occurs. It states that Zone C vehicles, areas with lower temperature cycling and humidity, could be in service for an estimated 15-20 years before degradation occurs.
